Turandot. The final and most exotic opera by Giacomo Puccini, premiered in nineteen twenty-six, famously incomplete at the composer's death and finished by Franco Alfano. Set in imperial China, it tells of an ice-hearted princess who has vowed to marry only the man who can answer three riddles and execute all who fail. The opera is celebrated for its grandiose oriental spectacle, memorable melodies, and the tenor aria Nessun Dorma, None shall sleep, one of the world's most recognizable opera songs.

The plot follows Calaf, an exiled prince who falls instantly in love with Princess Turandot and accepts her deadly challenge despite warnings from his loyal servant Liu. Nessun Dorma has transcended opera; it was featured in the nineteen ninety FIFA World Cup and has become a crossover standard, performed by singers across genres from Pavarotti to contemporary pop artists.

Puccini drew inspiration from Carlo Gozzi's eighteenth-century commedia dell'arte play, adapting its fantastical setting and romantic overcoming-the-obstacle plot. The score emphasizes orchestral grandeur and exotic sonic effects—pentatonic melodies, percussion coloration, and harmonic language attempting to evoke oriental sounds, though these are Puccini's interpretations rather than historically authentic Chinese music.

Liu, Calaf's devoted servant and a source of emotional counterweight to the ice-princess plot, has one of opera's most heartbreaking scenes and vocal lines. The three riddles themselves create operatic tension: they represent not just intellectual contests but the psychological battle between Turandot's coldness and Calaf's passionate love.

The opera was left unfinished with Puccini's death and completed by Franco Alfano, though modern productions sometimes restore Puccini's original sketches and cut Alfano's additions. Puccini died with the final duet between Calaf and Turandot incomplete; Alfano's conclusion is often controversial, with some arguing it betrays Puccini's style or emotional trajectory. It stands as Puccini's most ambitious work structurally and dramatically, blending his melodic gift with an almost Wagnerian scale of orchestral storytelling.

The opera's orientalism, while musically effective, reflects early-twentieth-century Western fantasies about China rather than authentic historical music or culture, making it a fascinating case study in how Western art depicts the exotic other.
